reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord that classically produces a dissociated sensory loss, with impaired pain and temperature but preserved light touch and proprioception
The dissociated sensory loss often has a cape-like distribution over the shoulders and arms as the central cord and crossing spinothalamic fibres are affected first
Painless burns or injuries and neuropathic joint degeneration (Charcot joints) can result from the loss of protective pain sensation
Progressive lower motor neuron signs in the hands and arms occur as the syrinx expands into the anterior horns
Frequently associated with a Chiari I malformation at the craniocervical junction, and also with prior trauma, tumour, or arachnoiditis
MRI of the whole spine and craniocervical junction is the definitive investigation and defines the syrinx and any underlying cause
Management targets the underlying cause, for example posterior fossa decompression for Chiari-associated syrinx, rather than the cavity alone
Extension of the cavity into the brainstem (syringobulbia) can cause lower cranial nerve and bulbar dysfunction
reference.pathophysiology: Syringomyelia is characterised by a longitudinal cavity within the spinal cord that disrupts neural tissue from the centre outward. Altered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, often related to obstruction at the craniocervical junction as in Chiari I malformation, are thought to drive fluid accumulation and cavity expansion. The central location preferentially damages the decussating spinothalamic fibres, producing dissociated sensory loss, and progressive enlargement affects anterior horn cells, long tracts, and autonomic pathways.
additionalDifferentials: Motor neuron disease when lower motor neuron hand wasting predominates
Leprosy and other causes of dissociated sensory loss
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the entire spine and craniocervical junction to define the syrinx and identify Chiari malformation or other cause
MRI of the brain to assess the posterior fossa and hindbrain
Contrast-enhanced imaging when an underlying tumour is suspected
CSF flow studies in selected cases to assess craniocervical junction dynamics
Neurophysiological studies where the differential includes motor neuron disease or neuropathy
redFlags: Rapid neurological deterioration or new bulbar symptoms from syringobulbia requiring urgent neurosurgical assessment
Progressive weakness, sensory loss, or sphincter disturbance indicating cord compromise
Associated Chiari malformation with brainstem compression signs
An underlying spinal cord tumour presenting as a secondary syrinx
reference.prognosis: Syringomyelia often progresses slowly over years, with a stepwise or gradual accumulation of deficits. Treating the underlying cause, particularly decompressing a Chiari malformation, can stabilise or improve symptoms, but established neurological deficits may not fully reverse and some patients continue to deteriorate despite surgery.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise dissociated sensory loss and its localising value
Overlooking an associated Chiari malformation or underlying tumour as the treatable cause
Attributing hand wasting solely to motor neuron disease without imaging the cord
Not counselling patients about protecting insensate areas from burns and injury
